findings.title: Working-hours check sets end equal to start, ignoring event length
findings.body: In the newly added working-hours branch of `checkIfIsAvailable`, the local `end` variable is computed as `slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute()`, which is identical to `start`. The intent (from the variable names and the surrounding comment `slot is outside of working hours`) was clearly to compare the slot's end time against `workingHour.endTime`. With `end === start` the predicate reduces to `if (start < workingHour.startTime || start > workingHour.endTime)`, so any slot whose start is still within working hours is treated as available even when the booking length pushes the slot past `workingHour.endTime`. Concretely: a 60‑minute event starting at 16:30 with working hours 9:00–17:00 (the slot ends at 17:30, past the working hours) would be returned as bookable.

findings.title: Date-override day comparison mixes local-mode and UTC-mode dayjs objects
findings.body: The comparison `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes").format("YYYY MM DD") === slotStartTime.format("YYYY MM DD")` is incorrect: `dayjs(date.start).add(...)` returns a Dayjs in the default (system local) timezone, so its `.format("YYYY MM DD")` is rendered in the server's local timezone, while `slotStartTime = time.utc()` is explicitly in UTC mode and formats in UTC. As a result the comparison only matches when the server happens to run in UTC (or in the same offset as the override), and silently fails in any other deployment timezone, causing date overrides to be missed entirely or applied on the wrong day. Both sides must use `.tz(organizerTimeZone)` (e.g. `dayjs(date.start).tz(organizerTimeZone).format("YYYY MM DD") === slotStartTime.tz(organizerTimeZone).format("YYYY MM DD")`), or both must be forced to UTC with `.utc()`.

findings.title: Date-override offset formula does not compute wall-clock time in invitee tz
findings.body: The new block computes `const offset = inviteeUtcOffset - organizerUtcOffset;` and then `dayjs(override.start).utc().add(offset, "minute").hour() / .minute()` to derive `startTime`/`endTime`. This does not produce the minute-of-day in the invitee's timezone. Worked example: override at 14:00 IST is stored as `override.start = 1970-01-01T08:30:00.000Z`. With invitee in Asia/Dhaka (+06:00) the code gives `offset = 30`, then `dayjs(08:30Z).utc().add(30m).hour() = 9`, so `startTime = 540` (09:00), i.e. slots appear at 09:00 Asia/Dhaka = 03:00 UTC. The correct value is `14:30 Asia/Dhaka = 08:30 UTC`, which would come from `dayjs(override.start).tz(timeZone).hour()*60 + .minute()`. As a result, for the production data shape (UTC moment encoding the organizer's wall clock) the PR silently shifts all date-override slots by the full timezone offset between organizer and invitee (e.g. 5h30m for IST→UTC, 5h for IST→EST).

findings.title: Date-override test uses literal-UTC times instead of organizer wall-clock times
findings.body: The `IstWorkHoursWithDateOverride` fixture stores the override as `{ startTime: "1970-01-01T14:00:00.000Z", endTime: "1970-01-01T18:00:00.000Z" }` and a schedule timeZone of `+05:30`, but the test's own name comment says the override is "2PM to 6PM IST". In production a Cal.com date override is the UTC moment that represents the organizer's local wall clock, so a 14:00 IST override is stored as `1970-01-01T08:30:00.000Z`. The fixture instead stores the literal UTC time 14:00, which happens to make the buggy `offset = inviteeUtcOffset - organizerUtcOffset` formula in `packages/lib/slots.ts` produce the right UTC slots by accident (both IST and Asia/Dhaka invitees see `08:30Z`). The new "different timezone" sub-assertion only verifies that the two invitees see the same UTC slot list; it does not exercise the real production shape where the stored Date represents the organizer's wall clock. With the production shape the PR's formula would emit slots shifted by the full organizer↔invitee offset and the tests would fail, so this gap is hiding the high-severity timezone bug above.
